tldr: This thread is a reading list of LLM research grouped by shared wording, not one event. From Oct 25 it ran from agent evaluation and model-control methods through compression papers and Anthropic's Nov 2 provable-inference update to knowledge editing and unlearning, then to Nov 10 studies of rater drift on Chatbot Arena and framing effects in LLM judgments.
whats_new: Nov 11: ShadowBench argues factual-recall evaluation relies almost entirely on explicit entity names, and its title claims that hides lexical anchoring and an "illusion of forgetting" in LLMs.
why_it_matters: Most items are single unreplicated preprints, but three recurring topics touch production: whether unlearning and knowledge edits remove knowledge or only its name-keyed recall, whether human-preference evals stay comparable over time, and what quantization and pruning cost in quality.

beats.headline: Agent evaluation and model control: long-horizon search, neuron steering, real-time vulnerability screening
beats.summary: Opening papers cover self-evolving decentralized multi-agent systems, a web-search benchmark that localizes the failing step, and replay for continual learning.

beats.headline: Efficiency work: Hessian-guided quantization, extreme-sparsity pruning and an early-stopping audit
beats.summary: The same days add RL-incentivized self-learning, a text-to-SQL survey and WeChat's production retrieval framework.

beats.headline: Anthropic reports progress on zkSNARK-based provable inference
beats.summary: The thread's only lab-published item: cryptographic proofs applied to LLM inference.

beats.headline: Updating what models know: answerability drift, multimodal unlearning and lifelong knowledge editing
beats.summary: Also here: an LLM choosing federated aggregation rules, and a security report on a framework targeting AI infrastructure.

beats.headline: Judgment under scrutiny: rising rater standards on Chatbot Arena, framing effects and personality benchmarks
beats.summary: These days also bring an LLM AutoML searcher, physics-guided fault diagnosis, a training-simulation benchmark and a cognitive account of learning by thinking.

beats.headline: ShadowBench questions name-based recall tests and whether models really forget
beats.summary: A single preprint that returns to the Nov 3-6 unlearning and editing topic from the evaluation side.

open_questions: Do published unlearning or knowledge-editing methods still pass when probed without explicit entity names, as ShadowBench's framing suggests they may not?
Do post-training updates from knowledge editing or unlearning keep a model's answerability judgments aligned with what it can answer?
Do Chatbot Arena or other human-preference leaderboards adjust rankings for the rater drift the Nov 10 study describes?
Does Anthropic publish proving cost or latency figures for zkSNARK-based provable inference?
Does the early-stopping audit identify a method that cuts reasoning tokens without lowering reliability?
Does RL-incentivized self-learning beat plain RAG on knowledge-intensive tasks in unfamiliar domains when replicated?
take_for_builders: Before signing off an unlearning or knowledge-edit change, test recall with prompts that describe the entity without naming it; treat these preprints as unreplicated reading, not deployment guidance.
